document.title: Science Grade Level Content Expectations (K-7)

29F96BB0DFE6013179D368A86D17958E.description: Identify Earth materials (air, water, soil) that are used to grow plants.

29F92610DFE6013179D268A86D17958E.description: Earth Materials- Earth materials that occur in nature include rocks, minerals, soils, water, and the gases of the atmosphere. Some Earth materials have properties which sustain plant and animal life.

29F8DB10DFE6013179D168A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard E.SE: Develop an understanding of the properties of earth materials and how those properties make materials useful. Understand gradual and rapid changes in earth materials and features of the surface of Earth. Understand magnetic properties of Earth.

29F7DEB0DFE6013179CE68A86D17958E.description: Identify and compare living and nonliving things.

29F78C30DFE6013179CD68A86D17958E.description: Identify that living things have basic needs.

29F74210DFE6013179CC68A86D17958E.description: Life Requirements- Organisms have basic needs. Animals and plants need air, water, and food. Plants also require light. Plants and animals use food as a source of energy and as a source of building material for growth and repair.

29F70100DFE6013179CB68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard L.OL: Develop an understanding that plants and animals (including humans) have basic requirements for maintaining life which include the need for air, water and a source of energy. Understand that all life forms can be classified as producers, consumers, or decomposers as they are all part of a global food chain where food/energy is supplied by plants which need light to produce food/energy. Develop an understanding that plants and animals can be classified by observable traits and physical characteristics. Understand that all living organisms are composed of cells and they exhibit cell growth and division. Understand that all plants and animals have a definite life cycle, body parts, and systems to perform specific life functions.

29F63E90DFE6013179C868A86D17958E.description: Observe how shape (for example: cone, cylinder, sphere), size, and weight of an object can affect motion.

29F5F620DFE6013179C768A86D17958E.description: Observe how pushes and pulls can change the speed or direction of moving objects.

29F5A070DFE6013179C668A86D17958E.description: Observe that objects initially at rest will move in the direction of the push or pull.

29F4FB70DFE6013179C468A86D17958E.description: Force- A force is either a push or a pull. The motion of objects can be changed by forces. The size of the change is related to the size of the force. The change is also related to the weight (mass) of the object on which the force is being exerted. When an object does not move in response to a force, it is because another force is being applied by the environment.

29F4B2E0DFE6013179C368A86D17958E.description: Observe how objects fall toward the earth.

29F46C80DFE6013179C268A86D17958E.description: Gravity- Earth pulls down on all objects with a force called gravity. With very few exceptions, objects fall to the ground no matter where the object is on the Earth.

29F42660DFE6013179C168A86D17958E.description: Describe the motion of an object (for example: away from or closer to) from different observers' views.

29F3DA10DFE6013179C068A86D17958E.description: Compare the position of an object (for example: above, below, in front of, behind, on) in relation to other objects around it.

29F39A30DFE6013179BF68A86D17958E.description: Position- A position of an object can be described by locating the object relative to other objects or a background. The description of the motion of an object from one observer's view may be different from that reported from a different observer's view.

29F35920DFE6013179BE68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard P.FM: Develop an understanding that the position and/or motion of an object is relative to a point of reference. Understand forces affect the motion and speed of an object and that the net force on an object is the total of all of the forces acting on it. Understand the Earth pulls down on objects with a force called gravity. Develop an understanding that some forces are in direct contact with objects, while other forces are not in direct contact with objects.

29F253D0DFE6013179BB68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate scientific concepts through various illustrations, performances, models, exhibits, and activities.

29F20780DFE6013179BA68A86D17958E.description: Reflecting on knowledge is the application of scientific knowledge to new and different situations. Reflecting on knowledge requires careful analysis of evidence that guides decision-making and the application of science throughout history and within society.

29F1C970DFE6013179B968A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.RS: Develop an understanding that claims and evidence for their scientific merit should be analyzed. Understand how scientists decide what constitutes scientific knowledge. Develop an understanding of the importance of reflection on scientific knowledge and its application to new situations to better understand the role of science in society and technology.

29F14DF0DFE6013179B768A86D17958E.description: Develop strategies for information gathering (ask an expert, use a book, make observations, conduct simple investigations, and watch a video).

29F10D10DFE6013179B668A86D17958E.description: Communicate and present findings of observations.

29F0C400DFE6013179B568A86D17958E.description: Share ideas about science through purposeful conversation.

29F07A20DFE6013179B468A86D17958E.description: Inquiry includes an analysis and presentation of findings that lead to future questions, research, and investigations.

29F03E80DFE6013179B368A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.IA: Develop an understanding that scientific inquiry and investigations require analysis and communication of findings, using appropriate technology.

29EFC400DFE6013179B168A86D17958E.description: Construct simple charts from data and observations.

29EF8480DFE6013179B068A86D17958E.description: Make accurate measurements with appropriate (non-standard) units for the measurement tool.

29EF4210DFE6013179AF68A86D17958E.description: Manipulate simple tools (for example: hand lens, pencils, balances, non-standard objects for measurement) that aid observation and data collection.

29EE5360DFE6013179AC68A86D17958E.description: Make purposeful observation of the natural world using the appropriate senses.

29EE03D0DFE6013179AB68A86D17958E.description: Inquiry involves generating questions, conducting investigations, and developing solutions to problems through reasoning and observation.

29EDBB60DFE6013179AA68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.IP: Develop an understanding that scientific inquiry and reasoning involves observing, questioning, investigating, recording, and developing solutions to problems

2D455EB0DFE60131810F68A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of selected critical elements of movement concepts while performing the following manipulative skills: roll, underhand throw, and overhand throw in isolated settings.

2D44BF10DFE60131810D68A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of selected movement concepts while performing locomotor skills: walk, run, leap, jump, skip, hop, gallop, slide, chase, flee, and dodge in isolated settings.

2D440E00DFE60131810B68A86D17958E.description: apply limited critical elements of the following non-locomotor skills: balancing, bending, stretching, rocking, rolling, curling, twisting, turning, pushing, pulling, swinging, swaying, and landing in isolated settings.

2D42F3F0DFE60131810868A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of critical elements of all movement concepts while performing selected manipulative skills (e.g., roll, underhand throw, and overhand throw) in isolated settings.

2D42A320DFE60131810768A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of critical elements of all movement concepts while performing non-locomotor skills in isolated settings.

2D425AC0DFE60131810668A86D17958E.description: apply knowledge of critical elements of all movement concepts while performing locomotor skills in isolated settings.

2D41C6F0DFE60131810468A86D17958E.description: use feedback from teachers and peers to improve motor skills and movement patterns, fitness, and physical activities in isolated settings.

2D40C5C0DFE60131810168A86D17958E.description: demonstrate use of selected on-the-object tactical movements of infield base positions and off-the-object problems of defending space and defending bases during modified striking/fielding games (e.g., strike a stationary object without a catcher, 4 vs. 4).

2D3FA9D0DFE6013180FD68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate use of selected on-the-ball and off-the-ball tactical movements for maintaining possession (e.g., passing, receiving), penetration/attack (e.g., shooting, moving with the object), and starting/restarting play (e.g., kick-off, throw-ins) during modified invasion games (e.g., small-sided games, such as 2 vs. 2).

2D3EF300DFE6013180FB68A86D17958E.description: demonstrate limited use of selected strategies for tactical problems, such as accuracy in distance and direction during modified, unopposed target games.

2D3E55C0DFE6013180F968A86D17958E.description: demonstrate ability to safely manipulate or use equipment in selected outdoor pursuits in isolated settings.

2D3E0910DFE6013180F868A86D17958E.description: demonstrate use of non-locomotor skills in outdoor pursuits with self and equipment in isolated settings.

2D3DAAC0DFE6013180F768A86D17958E.description: demonstrate use of locomotor skils in outdoor pursuits with self and equipment (e.g., backpack) in isolated settings.

2D3D5940DFE6013180F668A86D17958E.description: demonstrate use of movement concepts in outdoor pursuits with self and equipment in isolated settings.

2D3CB500DFE6013180F468A86D17958E.description: demonstrate the reversal of rhythmic locomotor patterns and change of direction.

2D3C1E50DFE6013180F268A86D17958E.description: demonstrate jumping or stepping from the side while wearing a life jacket and locomote to a position of safety in isolated settings.

document.title: MI Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

305A9550DFE6013186FA68A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

305A3F90DFE6013186F968A86D17958E.description: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
comments: Example: express 3 in the form 3 = 3/1; recognize that 6/1 = 6.
Example: locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point of a number line diagram.

3059F1A0DFE6013186F868A86D17958E.description: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., 1/2 = 2/4, 4/6 = 2/3). Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

30598810DFE6013186F768A86D17958E.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.

305943C0DFE6013186F668A86D17958E.description: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.

30590020DFE6013186F568A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction a/b on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths 1/b from 0. Recognize that the resulting interval has size a/b and that its endpoint locates the number a/b on the number line.

3058BC20DFE6013186F468A86D17958E.description: Represent a fraction 1/b on a number line diagram by defining the interval from 0 to 1 as the whole and partitioning it into b equal parts. Recognize that each part has size 1/b and that the endpoint of the part based at 0 locates the number 1/b on the number line.

30587850DFE6013186F368A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.

30583130DFE6013186F268A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a fraction a/b as the quantity formed by a parts of size 1/b.

3057DEB0DFE6013186F168A86D17958E.description: Develop understanding of fractions as numbers.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

30575DB0DFE6013186EF68A86D17958E.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
comments: For example, partition a shape into 4 parts with equal area, and describe the area of each part as 1/4 of the area of the shape.

30571D60DFE6013186EE68A86D17958E.description: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.

3056DF60DFE6013186ED68A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

30564F10DFE6013186EB68A86D17958E.description: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.

3055F590DFE6013186EA68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.

3055A240DFE6013186E968A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

30555C10DFE6013186E868A86D17958E.description: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths a and b + c is the sum of a × b and a × c. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.

30551A40DFE6013186E768A86D17958E.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.

3054D730DFE6013186E668A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.

30549010DFE6013186E568A86D17958E.description: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.

30542BE0DFE6013186E468A86D17958E.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft, and improvised units).

3053BF90DFE6013186E368A86D17958E.description: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by n unit squares is said to have an area of n square units.

30537230DFE6013186E268A86D17958E.description: A square with side length 1 unit, called "a unit square," is said to have "one square unit" of area, and can be used to measure area.

30531E10DFE6013186E168A86D17958E.description: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.

3052A510DFE6013186E068A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of area and relate area to multiplication and to addition.

305183A0DFE6013186DC68A86D17958E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with halves and fourths of an inch. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units— whole numbers, halves, or quarters.

30513000DFE6013186DB68A86D17958E.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step "how many more" and "how many less" problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
comments: For example, draw a bar graph in which each square in the bar graph might represent 5 pets.
Excludes multiplicative comparison problems (problems involving notions of "times as much";
Excludes compound units such as cm³ and finding the geometric volume of a container.
30524E00DFE6013186DF68A86D17958E.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.

305207E0DFE6013186DE68A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in minutes. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.

3051C6F0DFE6013186DD68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and estimation of intervals of time, liquid volumes, and masses of objects.

30503280DFE6013186D868A86D17958E.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10—90 (e.g., 9 × 80, 5 × 60) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

304FF1B0DFE6013186D768A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

304FB150DFE6013186D668A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.

304F6E00DFE6013186D568A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.
comments: A range of algorithms may be used.

304F24F0DFE6013186D468A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

304ED730DFE6013186D368A86D17958E.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
comments: For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.

304E8B40DFE6013186D268A86D17958E.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
comments: This standard is limited to problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers; students should know how to perform operations in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).

304E4300DFE6013186D168A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.

304DFE40DFE6013186D068A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that 8 × 5 = 40, one knows 40 ÷ 5 = 8) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.

304D6DA0DFE6013186CE68A86D17958E.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
comments: For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

304D1790DFE6013186CD68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
Example: Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.)

Example: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.)

304CD400DFE6013186CC68A86D17958E.description: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.

304C8C70DFE6013186CB68A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 × ? = 48, 5 = ÷ 3, 6 × 6 = ?.

304C4560DFE6013186CA68A86D17958E.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

304BF390DFE6013186C968A86D17958E.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.

304BA320DFE6013186C868A86D17958E.description: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7 objects each.
comments: For example, describe a context in which a total number of objects can be expressed as 5 × 7.

304B3890DFE6013186C768A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.

304AA7F0DFE6013186C568A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
304A5AC0DFE6013186C468A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
30491350DFE6013186C068A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
30483080DFE6013186BE68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Grade Level Content Expectations for Health Education (K-8)

32F95BE0DFE601318C1668A86D17958E.description: Explain how culture, media, and others influence what one thinks about oneself and relationships.

32F8C4E0DFE601318C1468A86D17958E.description: Describe criteria to determine whether resources provide accurate information about puberty; and apply these criteria to identify valid resources.

32F83CB0DFE601318C1268A86D17958E.description: Describe the functions of basic male and female reproductive anatomy.

32F7F560DFE601318C1168A86D17958E.description: Describe the menstrual cycle and its potential for human reproduction.

32F7A2F0DFE601318C1068A86D17958E.description: Describe how sperm cells are produced.

32F75C20DFE601318C0F68A86D17958E.description: Define the functions of sperm and egg cells in human reproduction.

32F71440DFE601318C0E68A86D17958E.description: Define and identify basic male and female reproductive anatomy using scientific names.

32F6D0F0DFE601318C0D68A86D17958E.description: Explain physical changes that occur during puberty (e.g., body hair, body odor, voice, body shape, strength, hormones, and menstruation).

32F68CF0DFE601318C0C68A86D17958E.description: Explain emotional changes during puberty (e.g., mood shifts).

32F64760DFE601318C0B68A86D17958E.description: Explain social changes during puberty (e.g., changes in friendships, crushes/attractions, and changing expectations of parents/adults).

32F5ED00DFE601318C0A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that males and females develop at different rates, and there are wide variations within each sex.

32F501C0DFE601318C0768A86D17958E.description: Describe ways people can protect themselves from infection with serious blood borne communicable diseases, including not touching blood, not touching used needles, and not having sex.

32F459A0DFE601318C0568A86D17958E.description: Describe how HIV is and is not transmitted.

32F406F0DFE601318C0468A86D17958E.description: Explain that it is safe to be a friend of someone who is living with HIV or AIDS.

32F23940DFE601318BFE68A86D17958E.description: Develop a plan to keep the body clean.

32F2E070DFE601318C0068A86D17958E.description: Analyze media influences related to hygiene products.

32F1AC30DFE601318BFC68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the physical, emotional, mental, and social importance of keeping the body clean.

32F04390DFE601318BF768A86D17958E.description: Advocate for a caring school environment.

DC9235D6D06D4126A777165D38953C6D.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

A0947207EE6A4D068F42C963788F2405.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

585638DCEC4644FD90D951C1FABA924C.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

78B3388324B04AB2B17013E40DAEA9EC.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Science Grade Level Content Expectations (K-7)

2A2D86E0DFE601317A4E68A86D17958E.description: Describe the major bodies of water on the Earth's surface (lakes, ponds, oceans, rivers, streams).

2A2D4170DFE601317A4D68A86D17958E.description: Describe how rain collects on the surface of the Earth and flows downhill into bodies of water (streams, rivers, lakes, oceans) or into the ground.

2A2CFF80DFE601317A4C68A86D17958E.description: Water Movement- Water moves in predictable patterns.

2A2CBED0DFE601317A4B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the properties (hard, visible, freezing, ice) of water as a solid (ice, snow, iceberg, sleet, hail).

2A2C7E10DFE601317A4A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the properties (visible, flowing, melting, dew) of water as a liquid (lakes, rivers, streams, oceans).

2A2C3B30DFE601317A4968A86D17958E.description: Identify household uses of water (drinking, cleaning, food preparation).

2A2BF4F0DFE601317A4868A86D17958E.description: Identify water sources (wells, springs, lakes, rivers, oceans).

2A2BA3F0DFE601317A4768A86D17958E.description: Water- Water is a natural resource and is found under the ground, on the surface of the earth, and in the sky. It exists in three states (liquid, solid, gas) and can go back and forth from one form to another.

2A2B5820DFE601317A4668A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard E.FE: Develop an understanding that Earth is a planet nearly covered with water and that water on Earth can be found in three states, solid, liquid, and gas. Understand how water on Earth moves in predictable patterns. Understand Earth's atmosphere as a mixture of gases and water vapor.

2A2AC2F0DFE601317A4468A86D17958E.description: Describe the major landforms of the surface of the Earth (mountains, plains, plateaus, valleys, hills).

2A2A74B0DFE601317A4368A86D17958E.description: Surface Changes- The surface of Earth changes. Some changes are due to slow processes, such as erosion and weathering, and some changes are due to rapid processes, such as landslides, volcanic eruptions, and earthquakes.

2A2A2AA0DFE601317A4268A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard E.SE: Develop an understanding of the properties of earth materials and how those properties make materials useful. Understand gradual and rapid changes in earth materials and features of the surface of Earth. Understand magnetic properties of Earth.

2A295560DFE601317A3F68A86D17958E.description: Identify characteristics of plants (for example: leaf shape, flower type, color, size) that are passed on from parents to young.

2A290F70DFE601317A3E68A86D17958E.description: Observable Characteristics- Plants and animals share many, but not all, characteristics of their parents.

2A28C560DFE601317A3D68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard L.HE: Develop an understanding that all life forms must reproduce to survive. Understand that characteristics of mature plants and animals may be inherited or acquired and that only inherited traits are passed on to their young. Understand that inherited traits can be influenced by changes in the environment and by genetics.

2A281B50DFE601317A3B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the life cycle of familiar flowering plants including the following stages: seed, plant, flower, and fruit.

2A27DAE0DFE601317A3A68A86D17958E.description: Life Cycles- Plants and animals have life cycles. Both plants and animals begin life and develop into adults, reproduce, and eventually die. The details of this life cycle are different for different organisms.

2A275850DFE601317A3868A86D17958E.description: Life Requirements- Organisms have basic needs. Animals and plants need air, water, and food. Plants also require light. Plants and animals use food as a source of energy and as a source of building material for growth and repair.

2A2712E0DFE601317A3768A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard L.OL: Develop an understanding that plants and animals (including humans) have basic requirements for maintaining life which include the need for air, water and a source of energy. Understand that all life forms can be classified as producers, consumers, or decomposers as they are all part of a global food chain where food/energy is supplied by plants which need light to produce food/energy. Develop an understanding that plants and animals can be classified by observable traits and physical characteristics. Understand that all living organisms are composed of cells and they exhibit cell growth and division. Understand that all plants and animals have a definite life cycle, body parts, and systems to perform specific life functions.

2A2631F0DFE601317A3468A86D17958E.description: Classify objects as single substances (ice, silver, sugar, salt) or mixtures (salt and pepper, mixed dry beans).

2A25E710DFE601317A3368A86D17958E.description: Material Composition- Some objects are composed of a single substance, while other objects are composed of more than one substance.

2A254D10DFE601317A3168A86D17958E.description: Measure the volume of liquids using common measuring tools (measuring cups, measuring spoons).

2A243970DFE601317A2D68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard P.PM: Develop an understanding that all matter has observable attributes with physical and chemical properties that are described, measured, and compared Understand that states of matter exist as solid, liquid, or gas; and have physical and chemical properties. Understand all matter is composed of combinations of elements, which are organized by common attributes and characteristics on the Periodic Table. Understand that substances can be classified as mixtures or compounds and according to their physical and chemical properties.

2A2379F0DFE601317A2A68A86D17958E.description: Identify technology used in everyday life.

2A233630DFE601317A2968A86D17958E.description: Use evidence when communicating scientific ideas.

2A22C790DFE601317A2868A86D17958E.description: Recognize that when a science investigation is done the way it was done before, similar results are expected.

2A228390DFE601317A2768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate scientific concepts through various illustrations, performances, models, exhibits, and activities.

2A2243D0DFE601317A2668A86D17958E.description: Reflecting on knowledge is the application of scientific knowledge to new and different situations. Reflecting on knowledge requires careful analysis of evidence that guides decision-making and the application of science throughout history and within society.

2A220550DFE601317A2568A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.RS: Develop an understanding that claims and evidence for their scientific merit should be analyzed. Understand how scientists decide what constitutes scientific knowledge. Develop an understanding of the importance of reflection on scientific knowledge and its application to new situations to better understand the role of science in society and technology.

2A218580DFE601317A2368A86D17958E.description: Develop strategies and skills for information gathering and problem solving (books, internet, ask an expert, observation, investigation, technology tools).

2A214020DFE601317A2268A86D17958E.description: Communicate and present findings of observations.

2A20EF60DFE601317A2168A86D17958E.description: Share ideas about science through purposeful conversation.

2A20ADD0DFE601317A2068A86D17958E.description: Inquiry includes an analysis and presentation of findings that lead to future questions, research, and investigations.

2A206BD0DFE601317A1F68A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.IA: Develop an understanding that scientific inquiry and investigations require analysis and communication of findings, using appropriate technology.

2A1FD6B0DFE601317A1D68A86D17958E.description: Construct simple charts and graphs from data and observations.

2A1F9590DFE601317A1C68A86D17958E.description: Make accurate measurements with appropriate units (meter, centimeter) for the measurement tool.

2A1F53A0DFE601317A1B68A86D17958E.description: Manipulate simple tools (ruler, meter stick, measuring cups, hand lens, thermometer, balance) that aid observation and data collection.

2A1E8580DFE601317A1868A86D17958E.description: Make purposeful observation of the natural world using the appropriate senses.

2A1E43E0DFE601317A1768A86D17958E.description: Inquiry involves generating questions, conducting investigations, and developing solutions to problems through reasoning and observation.

2A1E0170DFE601317A1668A86D17958E.description: K-7 Standard S.IP: Develop an understanding that scientific inquiry and reasoning involves observing, questioning, investigating, recording, and developing solutions to problems

334B6D00DFE601318CE568A86D17958E.description: Describe the importance of rest and sleep for personal health.

3349FD40DFE601318CE068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate using the problem solving steps to solve a problem.

document.title: Biology High School Content Expectations

2BFD98D0DFE601317E5468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and explain how biotechnology can improve a population and species.

2BFD41E0DFE601317E5368A86D17958E.description: Explain how changes at the gene level are the foundation for changes in populations and eventually the formation of new species.

2BFCDF50DFE601317E5268A86D17958E.description: Explain how evolution through natural selection can result in changes in biodiversity.

2BFC8EB0DFE601317E5168A86D17958E.description: Give examples of ways in which genetic variation and environmental factors are causes of evolution and the diversity of organisms.

2BFC3870DFE601317E5068A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of geographic isolation in speciation.

2BF8BC60DFE601317E4668A86D17958E.description: Explain how natural selection leads to organisms that are well suited for the environment (differential survival and reproduction of chance inherited variants, depending upon environmental conditions).

2BF86450DFE601317E4568A86D17958E.description: Explain how a new species or variety originates through the evolutionary process of natural selection.

2BF81760DFE601317E4468A86D17958E.description: Summarize the relationships between present-day organisms and those that inhabited the Earth in the past (e.g., use fossil record, embryonic stages, homologous structures, chemical basis).

2BF7CAF0DFE601317E4368A86D17958E.description: Describe how natural selection provides a mechanism for evolution.

2BF77E00DFE601317E4268A86D17958E.description: Summarize the major concepts of natural selection (differential survival and reproduction of chance inherited variants, depending on environmental conditions).

2BF6E120DFE601317E4068A86D17958E.description: Explain, with examples, that ecology studies the varieties and interactions of living things across space while evolution studies the varieties and interactions of living things across time. (prerequisite)

2BF63F60DFE601317E3E68A86D17958E.description: Explain the importance of the fossil record. (prerequisite)

2BF5E410DFE601317E3D68A86D17958E.description: Explain how extinction removes genes from the gene pool. (prerequisite)

2BF58380DFE601317E3C68A86D17958E.description: Define a population and identify local populations. (prerequisite)

2BF51B10DFE601317E3B68A86D17958E.description: Define a species and give examples. (prerequisite)

2BC0EBB0DFE601317DA068A86D17958E.description: Describe growth and development in terms of increase in cell number, cell size, and/or cell products. (prerequisite)

2BC09970DFE601317D9F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the importance of both water and the element carbon to cells. (prerequisite)

document.title: Social Studies Grade Level Content Expectations (K-8)

34DAE020DFE60131902E68A86D17958E.description: Participate in projects to help or inform others (e.g., service learning projects).

34DA8510DFE60131902D68A86D17958E.description: Engage in activities intended to contribute to solving a national or international problem studied.

34DA39C0DFE60131902C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate knowledge of how, when, and where individuals would plan and conduct activities intended to advance views in matters of public policy, report the results, and evaluate effectiveness.

34D9A640DFE60131902A68A86D17958E.description: Develop an action plan to address or inform others about the issue at the local to global scales.

34D95B90DFE60131902968A86D17958E.description: Compose a persuasive essay justifying the position with a reasoned argument.

34D90480DFE60131902868A86D17958E.description: Share and discuss findings of research and issue analysis in group discussions and debates.

34D88EA0DFE60131902768A86D17958E.description: Identify the causes and consequences and analyze the impact, both positive and negative.

34D83240DFE60131902668A86D17958E.description: Use inquiry methods to acquire content knowledge and appropriate data about the issue.

34D7E9D0DFE60131902568A86D17958E.description: Clearly state the issue as a question of public policy orally or in written form.

34D79F90DFE60131902468A86D17958E.description: Identify public policy issues related to global topics and issues studied.

34D74FD0DFE60131902368A86D17958E.description: Clearly state an issue as a question or public policy, trace the origins of an issue, analyze and synthesize various perspectives, and generate and evaluate alternative resolutions. Deeply examine policy issues in group discussions and debates to make reasoned and informed decisions. Write persuasive/argumentative essays expressing and justifying decisions on public policy issues. Plan and conduct activities intended to advance views on matters of public policy, report the results, and evaluate effectiveness.

34D667D0DFE60131902068A86D17958E.description: Explain and compare how economic systems (traditional, command, and market) answer four basic questions: What should be produced? How will it be produced? How will it be distributed? Who will receive the benefits of production? (e.g., market economies in Africa, Europe; command economy in North Korea; and the transition to market economies in Vietnam and China).

34D5D9E0DFE60131901E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how communications innovations have affected economic interactions and where and how people work (e.g., internet home offices, international work teams, international companies).

34D07630DFE60131900E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how governments address national issues and form policies, and how the policies may not be consistent with those of other countries (e.g., population pressures in China compared to Sweden; international immigration quotas, international aid, energy needs for natural gas and oil and military aid).

document.title: Physical Education Content Standards and Benchmarks

2C526FA0DFE601317EFA68A86D17958E.description: Accepts differences between idealized body images and elite performance levels portrayed by the media and their own personal characteristics and skills.

2C521380DFE601317EF968A86D17958E.description: Exhibits indicators of enjoyment for the aesthetic and creative aspects of skilled performance.

2C51BDE0DFE601317EF868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates Level 3 performance in the following:

2C517510DFE601317EF768A86D17958E.description: Recognizes physical activity as a positive opportunity for social interaction.

2C513230DFE601317EF668A86D17958E.description: Chooses to participate in activities that allow for self-expression.

2C50F4C0DFE601317EF568A86D17958E.description: Chooses to participate in activities that are personally challenging.

2C50B490DFE601317EF468A86D17958E.description: Chooses to exercise regularly outside of physical education for personal enjoyment and benefit.

2C506EE0DFE601317EF368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates Level 4 performance in the following:

2C502220DFE601317EF268A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (by the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents seek physical activity experiences for group membership and positive social interaction. They recognize and appreciate skilled performance. Physical activities provide a positive outlet for competition with peers and a means of gaining the respect and recognition of others. Physical activity can increase self-confidence and self-esteem as students discover renewed enjoyment in participation. Physical activity can provide confidence as students start to take steps toward independence. Challenge is found both in experiencing high levels of competition and in learning new and/or different activities. As students experience a greater awareness of feelings, the avenues of self-expression, provided by rhythmic movement, gymnastics, and other sport activities, become increasingly important.

2C4FE350DFE601317EF168A86D17958E.description: A physically educated person values physical activity for health, enjoyment, challenge, self-expression, and/or social interaction.

2C4FA410DFE601317EF068A86D17958E.description: Identifies key behaviors which exemplify the personal/social character traits of leadership.

2C4F62D0DFE601317EEF68A86D17958E.description: Exhibits behaviors which exemplify each of the following personal/social character traits: constructive competition, initiative, and leadership.

2C4F0E40DFE601317EEE68A86D17958E.description: Analyzes the benefits of possessing each of the following personal/social character traits: responsibility, best effort, cooperation, compassion, and leadership.

2C4EAB70DFE601317EED68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates Level 3 performance in the following:

2C4E6120DFE601317EEC68A86D17958E.description: Exhibits behaviors which exemplify each of the following personal/social character traits: responsibility, best effort, cooperation, and compassion.

2C4E2230DFE601317EEB68A86D17958E.description: Identifies key behaviors which exemplify each of the following personal/social character traits: responsibility, best effort, cooperation, and compassion.

2C4DE220DFE601317EEA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrates Level 4 performance in the following:

2C4D9810DFE601317EE968A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (by the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents begin to understand the concept of physical activity as a microcosm of modern culture and society. They recognize the role of physical activity in understanding diversity and continue to include and support each other, respecting the limitations and strengths of group members. Students move from merely identifying and following rules, procedures, safe practices, ethical behavior, and positive forms of social interaction to reflecting upon their role in physical activity settings and the benefits of physical activity. They have well-developed cooperation skills and are able to accomplish group/team goals in both cooperative and competitive activities. Adolescents seek greater independence from adults and effectively work independently and in groups to complete assigned tasks. They make appropriate decisions to resolve conflicts arising from the powerful influence of peers, and they practice appropriate problem-solving techniques to resolve conflicts, when necessary, in competitive activities.

2C4D4AA0DFE601317EE868A86D17958E.description: A physically educated person exhibits responsible personal and social behavior that respects self and others in physical activity settings.

2C4CFAD0DFE601317EE768A86D17958E.description: Monitors the effects of physical activity and nutrition on the body.

2C4CA7C0DFE601317EE668A86D17958E.description: Develops and implements a plan for improving or maintaining their health-related fitness status, with assistance from the teacher.

2C4C6170DFE601317EE568A86D17958E.description: Applies the physiological indicators associated with moderate to vigorous physical activity to monitor and/or adjust participation/effort (e.g., palpitating pulse, using pedometers and/or heart rate monitors to train in target heart rate zones).

2C4C1DE0DFE601317EE468A86D17958E.description: Recognizes the principles of training (e.g., Frequency, Intensity, Type, Time (F.I.T.T.), overload, specificity).

2C4B91F0DFE601317EE268A86D17958E.description: Meets criterion-referenced age- and gender-specific, health-related fitness standards for cardiorespiratory, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, and body composition (e.g., Fitnessgram, President's Challenge, and Brockport Physical Fitness Test).

2C4B4390DFE601317EE168A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (by the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents participate in moderate to vigorous physical activities on a regular basis without undue fatigue. They participate in physical activities that address each component of health-related fitness, including cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, and body composition. Students know the components of fitness and how these relate to their overall fitness status. Students monitor their own heart rate, breathing rate, perceived exertion, and recovery rate during and following strenuous physical activity. They assess their personal fitness status for each component and use this information to assist in development of individualized physical fitness goals, with little help from the teacher. Students show progress towards knowing the various principles of training (e.g., threshold, overload, specificity) and how these principles can be utilized in improving one's level of physical fitness.

2C4AF010DFE601317EE068A86D17958E.description: A physically educated person achieves and maintains a health-enhancing level of physical fitness.

2C4AA5D0DFE601317EDF68A86D17958E.description: Participating most days of the week in a variety of health-enhancing physical activities outside of physical education.

2C4A5910DFE601317EDE68A86D17958E.description: Participating primarily in physical activities that focus on combining locomotor and manipulative skills and applying strategies in modified game play.

2C4A0460DFE601317EDD68A86D17958E.description: Exploring a wide variety of target, net/wall, invasion, striking/fielding/running games; rhythmic activities; outdoor pursuits; and fitness-related activities in and outside of physical education.

2C49BAC0DFE601317EDC68A86D17958E.description: Accumulates time in physical activities that are moderate to vigorous in intensity while:

2C496F90DFE601317EDB68A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (by the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents are able to independently set physical activity goals and participate in individualized programs of physical activity and exercise based on personal goals and interests, as well as on the results of fitness assessments. They select and utilize practice procedures and training principles appropriate for the activity goals they set. Students have an increasing awareness of the opportunities for participation in a broad range of activities that may meet their needs and interests. They participate regularly in moderate to vigorous physical activities in both school and non-school settings.

2C4696C0DFE601317ED168A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (at the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents exhibit an increasingly complex discipline-specific knowledge. They can identify principles of practice and conditioning that enhance movement performance. They have higher levels of understanding and application of movement concepts/principles and game strategies, critical elements of activity-specific movement skills and characteristics representing highly skilled performance. Students know when, why, and how to use strategies and tactics within game play. They use information from a variety of sources, both internal and external, to guide and improve performance.

2C4654E0DFE601317ED068A86D17958E.description: A physically educated person demonstrates understanding of movement concepts, principles, strategies, and tactics as they apply to the learning and performance of physical activities.

2C4612D0DFE601317ECF68A86D17958E.description: Using tactics during modified game play.

2C443190DFE601317EC968A86D17958E.description: 6-8 Student expectations (at the end of grade 8)
comments: Adolescents are able to participate with skill in a variety of modified sports, rhythmic movement, gymnastics, and outdoor activities. Students achieve mature forms in the basic skills of the more specialized sports, rhythmic movement, gymnastics activities. They use the skills successfully in modified games or activities of increasing complexity and in combination with other basic skills. Students demonstrate use of tactics within sport activities.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
310D0580DFE60131881168A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

310CB900DFE60131881068A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

310B4FF0DFE60131880C68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
